Lecture 37

Heat and diffusion on bounded domains

Lecture objectives

We prove that the heat problem on an interval has at most one classical solution, solve it by separation of variables, and show how the series behaves for t>0t>0t>0 and as t→0+.t\to0^+t→0+. We then add fixed end temperatures and heat sources and write the solution with a kernel.

Lecture 29 derived the heat equation and fixed its classical solutions. Lecture 32 solved a string of finite length with sine series. In this lecture the same series describe heat flow in a uniform rod of finite length. The modes no longer oscillate. Each decays at its own rate, and rough initial temperatures become smooth at once. The lecture reads in four stages: uniqueness (Section 37.1), the series solution and a cooling rod (Sections 37.2–37.3), rough data and other ends (Section 37.4), and end temperatures and sources, then the kernel (Section 37.5).

37.4 Rough data and other ends

For piecewise continuous u0u_0u0​ that does not vanish at the ends, Theorem 37.2 still gives a function that solves the equation and the boundary conditions for t>0t>0t>0 and approaches u0u_0u0​ in the mean square. It is a solution in the following weaker sense.

Definition 37.4 (Solution with mean-square initial values). Let u0u_0u0​ be piecewise continuous on [0,L],[0,L][0,L], and let each end carry the condition u=0u=0u=0 or ux=0.u_x=0ux​=0. A solution with mean-square initial values is a function uuu on [0,L]×(0,∞)[0,L]\times(0,\infty)[0,L]×(0,∞) such that u,uu, ut,u_tut​, uxu_xux​ and uxxu_{xx}uxx​ are continuous there, one-sided at the ends, uuu solves ut=Duxxu_t=Du_{xx}ut​=Duxx​ and the end conditions for t>0,t>0t>0, and ∥u(⋅,t)−u0∥→0\norm{u(\cdot,t)-u_0}\to0∥u(⋅,t)−u0​∥→0 as t→0+.t\to0^+t→0+.

Proposition 37.5 (Uniqueness for mean-square initial values). For each u0u_0u0​ and each choice of end conditions there is at most one solution with mean-square initial values.

Proof. Let www be the difference of two such solutions, E(t)=∥w(⋅,t)∥2,E(t)=\norm{w(\cdot,t)}^2E(t)=∥w(⋅,t)∥2, and 0<t1<t2.0<t_1<t_20<t1​<t2​. The first term of (37.10) carries the initial temperature and the second the heat released at earlier times, as the two terms of Lecture 8’s complete solution carry the initial data and the forcing. Lecture 43 compares KKK with the diffusion kernel of the whole line.

Summary

On an interval the heat equation separates into modes that decay at the rates Dkn2.Dk_n^2Dkn2​. With no source and piecewise continuous initial data, the series is smooth for t>0t>0t>0 and takes its initial values in the mean square. It is classical when the data are continuous, piecewise C1C^1C1 and vanish at the ends, and an energy argument for the difference of two solutions shows that it is unique.

  • Uniqueness: at most one classical solution with Dirichlet, Neumann or mixed ends; at most one solution with mean-square initial values.

  • Series: u=∑nbn(u0)e−Dkn2tsin⁡(knx);u=\sum_nb_n(u_0)\ee^{-Dk_n^2t}\sin(k_nx)u=∑n​bn​(u0​)e−Dkn2​tsin(kn​x); smooth for t>0t>0t>0 for piecewise continuous u0,u_0u0​, and ∥u(⋅,t)∥≤e−t/tr∥u0∥\norm{u(\cdot,t)}\le\ee^{-t/t_{\mathrm r}}\norm{u_0}∥u(⋅,t)∥≤e−t/tr​∥u0​∥ with tr=L2/(π2D).t_{\mathrm r}=L^2/(\pi^2D)tr​=L2/(π2D).

  • Initial values: ∥u(⋅,t)−u0∥→0\norm{u(\cdot,t)-u_0}\to0∥u(⋅,t)−u0​∥→0 for piecewise continuous u0;u_0u0​; a classical solution for continuous piecewise C1C^1C1 u0u_0u0​ with u0(0)=u0(L)=0.u_0(0)=u_0(L)=0u0​(0)=u0​(L)=0.

  • Other ends: mixed ends by even reflection, modes sin⁡(μmx)\sin(\mu_mx)sin(μm​x) with μm=(m−12)π/L;\mu_m=(m-\frac12)\pi/Lμm​=(m−21​)π/L; insulated ends with cosines, a conserved mean and no condition on u0′.u_0'u0′​.

  • Equilibrium: subtract the steady state us;u_{\mathrm s}us​; the rest decays.

  • Sources: q˙n+Dkn2qn=gn;\dot q_n+Dk_n^2q_n=g_nq˙​n​+Dkn2​qn​=gn​; with insulated ends a uniform source raises the mean linearly; the kernel K(x,t;ξ,τ)K(x,t;\xi,\tau)K(x,t;ξ,τ) gives (37.10).

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Two classical solutions on 0<x<L0<x<L0<x<L have the same heat source, initial profile, prescribed temperature at the left end and prescribed slope at the right end. Their difference is www. Why does the lecture’s uniqueness proof replace w2w^2w2 by a function Pε(w)P_\varepsilon(w)Pε​(w) that vanishes for small ∣w∣\abs w∣w∣?

Hint. Check which derivative is known to extend to each end. The cutoff makes one boundary product vanish before taking its limit.

The difference has zero initial data and source, w(0,t)=0w(0,t)=0w(0,t)=0 and wx(L,t)=0w_x(L,t)=0wx​(L,t)=0. Integration by parts gives the boundary product Pε′(w)wxP_\varepsilon'(w)w_xPε′​(w)wx​. The function PεP_\varepsilonPε​ is constant near zero, so its derivative also vanishes for small ∣w∣\abs w∣w∣. Near the Dirichlet end, continuity of www makes the first factor zero without a boundary value for wxw_xwx​. At the Neumann end the second factor tends to zero. The nonnegative cutoff energy cannot increase and starts at zero, yielding uniqueness as the cutoff shrinks. The Dirichlet condition prescribes only the value of www. The common source cancels before the function is chosen.

2. A rod with no source has both ends held at zero temperature. Its initial profile is piecewise continuous with an interior jump. What does the sine-series heat solution guarantee?

Hint. Separate the damping for each fixed positive time from how the solution takes the initial data.

The mode factors are e−Dkn2t\ee^{-Dk_n^2t}e−Dkn2​t. On every time strip bounded away from zero they dominate the powers of knk_nkn​ introduced by differentiation, so the solution is smooth for positive time. The initial profile is recovered in mean square by the sine expansion and the limit of the modal factors. Uniform convergence to a function with an interior jump is impossible for these continuous profiles. A jump can occur in the initial data without preventing evolution, and positive-time smoothing removes it.

3. A source-free insulated rod has length L=π mL=\pi\,\mathrm mL=πm and diffusivity D=1 m2 s−1D=1\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}D=1m2s−1. Its initial temperature relative to a reference is u0(x)=3 K+(1 K)cos⁡(2πx/L)u_0(x)=3\,\mathrm K+(1\,\mathrm K)\cos(2\pi x/L)u0​(x)=3K+(1K)cos(2πx/L). How many seconds does its deviation from equilibrium take to decrease by a factor of e\eee? Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. The constant mode is the equilibrium. Identify the lowest nonconstant mode that is actually present.

The spatial mean is 3 K3\,\mathrm K3K and stays constant at insulated ends. The only nonconstant mode has wave number k2=2π/L=2 m−1k_2=2\pi/L=2\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}k2​=2π/L=2m−1. Its decay rate is Dk22=4 s−1Dk_2^2=4\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}Dk22​=4s−1. The reciprocal is 0.25 s0.25\,\mathrm s0.25s. The first nonconstant mode is allowed by the ends but has zero coefficient in these data.

4. A heat equation with homogeneous Dirichlet ends has a source in just one sine mode. In dimensionless variables its modal coordinate satisfies q˙+2q=8\dot q+2q=8q˙​+2q=8 with q(0)=0q(0)=0q(0)=0. Which coordinate gives the source-driven response?

Hint. In the forcing integral the decay factor depends on the time elapsed since the source acted.

The source contributes q(t)=8∫0te−2(t−τ) ⁣dτ=4(1−e−2t)q(t)=8\int_0^t\ee^{-2(t-\tau)}\dd\tau=4(1-\ee^{-2t})q(t)=8∫0t​e−2(t−τ)dτ=4(1−e−2t). The coordinate starts at zero and tends to the steady value 444. A pure exponential 4e−2t4\ee^{-2t}4e−2t describes decay from nonzero initial data with no source. The value 8(1−e−2t)8(1-\ee^{-2t})8(1−e−2t) misses the divisor from integration. The factor e−t\ee^{-t}e−t gives the wrong modal decay rate.
